data.title: Jump Game
data.summary:
Input: A list of non-negative integers representing the maximum jump length at each position.
Output: A boolean indicating if the last index is reachable starting from the first index.
Rules: Each element represents the maximum distance you can jump forward from that index.

data.key_insight: Maintain the maximum reachable index as you iterate through the array. If at any point your current index exceeds the maximum reachable index, you cannot proceed further and should return false.

steps.title: Initialize Max Reach
steps.detail: Set a variable 'max_reach' to 0, which tracks the furthest index we can currently reach.

steps.title: Iterate and Update
steps.detail: Loop through each index 'i' in the array. If 'i' is greater than 'max_reach', it means we cannot reach this index, so return false.

steps.title: Extend Reach
steps.detail: Update 'max_reach' to be the maximum of its current value and 'i + nums[i]'.

steps.title: Completion Check
steps.detail: If the loop finishes without returning false, it means we can reach or exceed the last index, so return true.

data.pattern_summary: Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step to find the global optimum. Reach for this pattern when checking if a target state can be reached by tracking the furthest possible progress from the current state.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We only need to maintain the furthest reachable index as we iterate through the list.

pattern_options.name: Depth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: DFS explores all paths which leads to exponential time complexity, whereas this problem only requires tracking a single reachability value.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers are useful for sorted arrays or scanning from both ends, but jumping requires scanning forward while maintaining a cumulative reach limit.

pattern_options.name: Sliding Window
pattern_options.feedback: Sliding windows are used for contiguous subarrays of fixed or dynamic size, not for jump sequences spanning variable distances.

signals.phrase: maximum jump length at each position
signals.hint: Indicates that each index gives you a range of future indices you can visit.

signals.phrase: indicating if the last index is reachable
signals.hint: Suggests we are tracking a boolean state of reachability from the start to the end.

data.brute_force_idea: Initialize a boolean array to track which indices are reachable, starting with only the first index as reachable. Iterate through every index, and if it is reachable, mark all subsequent indices within its jump range as reachable. Finally, check if the last index is marked as reachable.
data.brute_force_why: In the worst case, for each element we iterate through its maximum jump length which can be proportional to the array size n, leading to nested loops.
data.bottleneck: The inner loop explicitly checks and marks every single reachable index within the jump range, leading to redundant updates for indices we might have already processed.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how much state you need to remember to solve the problem.
Do you actually need to store reachability for every single index, or just the furthest index you can reach so far?
Think about whether you can solve this in a single pass by updating a single integer variable instead of an entire array.

data.overview: The algorithm uses a greedy approach to determine if the last index is reachable. It maintains the furthest possible index you can reach as you iterate through the array.
data.intuition: Think of it like having a fuel tank that gets refilled at each position. As you travel step by step, your remaining fuel expands whenever you find a larger jump capability, but if you ever reach a position beyond your current fuel range, you are stranded.

pitfalls: Forgetting to check if i > max_reach before updating max_reach.
Trying to simulate every possible path using backtracking, leading to Time Limit Exceeded.
Returning false prematurely before checking all reachable positions up to the current index.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach repeatedly scans ahead from every reachable index, leading to quadratic time. The optimized greedy approach discards the boolean array and instead tracks only the furthest index reachable at any given moment. If we ever encounter an index that exceeds our current maximum reach, we know we are stuck and can return False immediately.

derivation.note: Iterates through each element in the list exactly once via enumerate.
Checks if the current index is beyond the maximum reachable distance.
Updates the maximum reach using the current position and jump length.
Returns True if the loop finishes without getting stuck.

data.time_summary: Line 4 runs n times, and lines 5 and 7 execute once per iteration in constant time. The total step count scales linearly with the input size, supported by the measured evidence showing step counts scaling directly with n.
data.space_summary: Only a single integer variable max_reach is maintained regardless of input size, requiring constant O(1) extra space.
data.takeaway: When checking reachability or intervals, track the current boundary of what is possible dynamically in a single pass rather than simulating every individual path.
mistakes: Failing to check if the current index exceeds max_reach before updating it, which can miss dead ends.
Using nested loops to simulate every jump choice instead of maintaining a running maximum boundary.
Returning early with True inside the loop before verifying all visited steps.
